6. Course Description:
Over the last two and a half centuries, industrialization led to the clustering of manufacturing
hubs in areas with abundant energy resources that eventually evolved into cities. Food
production systems are currently suffering from the expansion of cities through the
encroachment on farmland and the declining populations of agrarian societies due to mass
human migration to cities. The demand for food for the ever-increasing world population is met
by adopting the mass-production model focused solely on farm output through mechanized
farming, intensive use of agrochemicals (fertilizers and pesticides), irrigation, and breeding
genetically superior plant varieties. The decline in arable land, poor soil-water health due to
excessive fertilizer use, over-dependence on genetically superior plant varieties, and the
demand for greater food production are among the critical challenges for humankind. Thus, a
sustainable, adaptive, and resilient agroecosystem design paradigm is needed, where all key
stakeholders, land (soil), water, plants, animals, energy, and farming communities, can be
brought under the unified umbrella of sustainability. This course aims to introduce design
students to emerging sustainable agrotechnologies and agricultural design paradigms, amid
climate extremes and population growth, that pivot on sustainability and local resilience.

6. Course Description:
The aim of this course is to provide a comprehensive foundation in cognitive human factors and
applied psychology for designers, enabling them to understand the scientific basis of human
behavior and use these principles to design. This course is envisioned as supplementing the content
of other existing courses from a psychological perspective in design, such as communication
design, interaction design, among others, and is not a replacement for any of these. This course
should ideally be taken alongside other design courses so that students can understand design
practice in the context of scientific principles of human behavior. The course will introduce the
principles of human behavior and its applicability in design problems. The course will present an
overview of the subject as well as direct students in case they wish to delve deeper into certain
areas using small design exercises or design projects.

Course Description:
Designers professionally work across independent practices like studios, consultancies, startups and
multidisciplinary teams in a corporate environment. Designing meaningful solutions for the users / society needs
to be complemented by ability to identify opportunities, engage with external clients, define projects scopes, plans
and manage design processes to create and communicate value upstream and downstream and eventually build
sustainable professional practice.

The course combines conceptual input, case discussions, practical exercises and a simulated consulting
engagement. It aims to equip future design entrepreneurs with the knowledge, tools and confidence to take steps
towards professional practice and build a sustainable design practice.

It exposes fresh designers to how professional design work is initiated, proposed, priced, organized,
communicated and delivered in real client contexts.

D) Short summary for including in the Courses of Study Booklet
Products have evolved by leaps and bounds in the last few decades, owing to technological innovations
and lifestyle changes. This in turn has put the spotlight on interactions between humans and the
products they use. The focus of this course is to develop capabilities to analyse and redesign the
nuances of human-product interactions, so as to make tasks easier, more effective and more enjoyable
for the target users. In this course, students work in groups to research and redesign a tangible product
from a usability perspective. The product could be a home/personal product (washing machine, sewing
machine, party speaker, DSLR, video camera, etc.), community/commercial product (treadmill, coffee
machine, projector, photocopy machine, vending machine, DJ console, etc.), medical product
(sonography machine, body composition analyser, ventilator, etc.) industrial product (paper cutting
machine, book binding machine, laser cutting machine, etc.) or vehicle control panel (bus, excavator,
road paving machine, etc.).

Rationale and Need for the Course
Policy impact on growth and welfare goes beyond the understanding of the partial
equilibrium models (A partial equilibrium model determines the equilibrium price and
quantity in a single market by considering only the demand and supply conditions of that
market, without accounting for interactions with the rest of the economy). The economic
channels through which policies impact growth and welfare are allocative and technical
efficiency, terms of trade, investment savings balance, endowment effects, preference
shifting impacts among others. Governments, international organizations and researchers
increasingly rely on computable general equilibrium models to evaluate trade
agreements, climate policies, carbon taxation, technological progress, energy transitions
and regional development strategies. The course equips students with theoretical and
practical skills required for policy-oriented research. A general equilibrium model is a
framework in which equilibrium is determined simultaneously across all goods, factor, and
institutional markets, taking into account the interdependence among economic agents and
sectors.

6. Course Description: Low-voltage, high-current power converter topologies are adopted in smartphones,
laptops, servers, network switches, etc. These power management systems include power circuits, gate drivers,
control circuits, and communication protocols. Therefore, a systems engineer in the power semiconductor
industry must develop a block-level understanding of complete power management integrated circuits (PMICs).
This course will introduce the students to the system specifications and how power electronic circuits and
peripherals are designed to meet those requirements.
This course is divided into ten modules and begins with an introduction to different power management
system requirements. This is followed by two fundamental modules focusing on synchronous buck and other
basic PWM converters. The subsequent two modules cover dynamic modeling and voltage-mode control of
PWM converters. The sixth module deals with block-level understanding of PMICs. The seventh module
discusses the PMBUS communication protocol. The last three course modules deal with advanced control
techniques and converter topologies, including multi-phase synchronous buck.

10. Course Description: Photonic devices and systems play a crucial role in diverse areas
ranging from modern communication, information processing, display, imaging, and
energy harvesting. To meet the current technological demands in these areas, photonic
systems have increasingly grown in complexity and functionality. Some of the notable
developments in recent years include Photonic integrated circuits (or Silicon photonics),
photonic accelerators for AI, AR/VR displays, and quantum communication networks.
This course aims to bridge the gap between the “abstract” Maxwell’s equations and the
building blocks of a photonic integrated circuit. The course starts with a discussion of
different formulations of the Maxwell’s equations, the general properties of its solutions,
and the commonly used techniques to determine these solutions. Building on these, the
course introduces the standard photonic structures such as dielectric waveguides, cavities,
and photonic crystals. Numerical simulation and visualization tools are frequently used to
better illustrate the concepts. The course concludes with a discussion of designing photonic
systems using these standard building blocks for a certain application.

6. Course Description:

A) Objectives:
Electron transport has long been central to microelectronics and VLSI. Each electron also carries spin
angular momentum, which can be harnessed for data storage and processing. This course introduces
the key principles of spin transport in heterostructures, providing students in Electrical Engineering
and related disciplines with the foundation needed to pursue research in this area. Beginning with a
review of essential quantum mechanics concepts, the course will gradually introduce the properties
of quantum materials and devices, including the coupling among charge, spin, and orbital degrees of
freedom and their interactions with magnons and phonons.

freedom and their interactions with magnons and phonons.
The course is organized into four modules. The first introduces the essential concepts of quantum
mechanics that provide the foundation for the course and will span 6–7 lectures. The second covers
the fundamentals of nanomagnetism over 6–7 lectures. The third focuses on the core concepts of
spintronics, including spin currents, spin torques, and spin-torque-induced magnetization dynamics.
Topics include spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance, magnetization switching, and oscillations,
covered over 8–9 lectures. The fourth module covers advanced topics, including spin–orbit coupling
effects, spintronic devices, and their applications.

In addition to standard homework exercises, students will undertake four mini-projects involving
macrospin and quantum simulations. These projects will help them connect the theoretical concepts
with physical behaviour and develop practical simulation skills. Students will also deliver a seminar
and submit a report on assigned research topics. The course is designed for students with limited prior
exposure to spintronics, guiding them from its basic principles to advanced concepts and practical
applications.

Course Description :

As MOSFETs scale, their architecture evolves to overcome increasingly fundamental limits in
electrostatics, transport, variability, and manufacturability. This course aims to develops the
device physics needed to understand the evolution from bulk MOSFETs to modern 3D transistors,
2D materials-based devices, and emerging More-than-Moore technologies.

ce physics needed to understand the evolution from bulk MOSFETs to modern 3D transistors,
2D materials-based devices, and emerging More-than-Moore technologies.
The course will begin with the review of MOSFET scaling and short-channel eﬀects, and examines
the architectural innovations developed to address them. It will progress from bulk MOSFETs to
PDSOI and FDSOI, FinFETs, nanosheet and nanowire FETs, and complementary FETs (CFETs).
The course will develop the fundamentals of electrostatics and carrier transport in thin and highly
conﬁned channels, including the eﬀects of geometry, conﬁnement, band structure, mobility,
defects, surface roughness, and device variability. Approaches for modeling and simulating these
eﬀects will also be introduced.

The course will then explores the atomic limit of channel scaling through 2D materials. It will
covers representative material systems such as graphene, transition-metal dichalcogenides
(TMDs), and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), focusing on their electronic properties i.e.
electrostatics, and transport. Particular attention will be given to the challenges of realizing
practical 2D devices, including contacts, gate dielectrics, substrates, defects and doping.

The course concludes with an introduction to More-than-Moore device concepts, such as
realizing new material system with 2D materials based hetro-integrations, leveraging the defect in
these materials to build new devices for neuromorphic computing, leveraging phase change and
spin to realise new devices, and other emerging device concepts for unconventional computing
and specialized applications.

The main objective is to develop an understanding of device physics beyond the bulk MOSFET
and the technological directions shaping future transistors. The course also aims to provide
students with a framework for analyzing emerging devices: identifying the physical limitations of a
device, understanding how its architecture addresses those limitations, evaluating the associated
trade-oﬀs, and developing informed ideas for new device concepts.

6. Course Description:

This course is designed for undergraduate students to provide an overview of the
significant ideas in Indian grammatical traditions. The primary focus of the course is to
highlight the distinct grammatical thought of India basing on the texts from the Vedic,
Classical Sanskrit, Prakrits, medieval Indian grammars to the grammars of modern Indian

istinct grammatical thought of India basing on the texts from the Vedic,
Classical Sanskrit, Prakrits, medieval Indian grammars to the grammars of modern Indian
languages. The course introduces the Vedic corpus relevant to the grammatical thought:
the Prātiśākhyas, Śikṣās, Nirukta, Vyākaraṇa, and other pre-Pāṇinian grammarians. The
course lays special emphasis on the selected ideas from Pāṇinian Grammar: Aṣṭādhyāyī
by introducing the basics of the grammar through actual interpretation and translation of
few sūtras. The course offers an outline of the Pāṇinian tradition: the Trimuni, and the
philosophical issues, linguistic debates in Bhartṛhari, other śāstra traditions. The course
goes on to trace the influence of Pāṇinian grammar on other Sanskrit grammars, Prakrit
grammars, and later (medieval and modern) grammars of Indic and Dravidian langauges
too. It is in this sense a course in intellectual history of Indian grammatical thought. The
course briefly discusses the influence the Indian grammatical tradition exerted on early

D) Short summary for including in the Courses of Study Booklet
ENG1XX This undergraduate course surveys major ideas in Indian grammatical traditions, from
the Vedic corpus and pre-Pāṇinian grammarians to classical Sanskrit, Prakrit, and modern
language grammars. Special emphasis is placed on Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, with hands-on
interpretation of selected sūtras, the Trimuni tradition, and linguistic debates in Bhartṛhari and
other śāstras. The course traces Pāṇini’s influence on later Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Dravidian
grammars, framing grammar as intellectual history. It also highlights resonances with early
modern linguistics on issues like prescriptivism vs. descriptivism, form vs. function, and basic
linguistic units. Students gain familiarity with India’s diverse yet interconnected grammatical
heritage.

6. Course Description
This course introduces Environmental Humanities (EH) as an interdisciplinary field that brings the
humanities into sustained conversation with environmental sciences and other modes of ecological
inquiry. It examines how literature, film, visual culture, digital media, philosophy, history, anthropology,
ethics and cultural practices shape understandings of nature, environment, climate and the more-than-
human world. The course asks how environmental crises are narrated, experienced, remembered and
contested, and how humanities perspectives can contribute to environmental thought, justice and possible
futures.

contested, and how humanities perspectives can contribute to environmental thought, justice and possible
futures.
The course begins by interrogating the nature–culture divide and the emergence of environmental
humanities, before moving through ecocriticism, environmental imagination, place and landscape, the
Anthropocene and its critical alternatives, environmental justice, postcolonial and decolonial ecologies,
ecofeminism, posthumanism, new materialism and multispecies studies. It further examines
environmental governance, ecological citizenship, Indigenous and traditional ecological knowledge
systems, environmental communication, and public humanities approaches to ecological challenges. It
also introduces focused approaches such as slow violence, toxicity and waste studies, Blue Humanities,
environmental memory, ecocinema, ecomedia, ecopoetics and speculative/climate fiction. Attention is
also given to contemporary concerns including extinction studies, energy humanities, disaster humanities,
urban ecologies, and digital environmental cultures.

Attention will be given to Indian and South Asian environmental contexts, including environmental

cultural politics of environmental change. Students will engage with literary texts, films, visual archives,

D) Short Summary for Courses of Study Booklet
An interdisciplinary introduction to Environmental Humanities, this course examines how literature, film,
visual culture, history, philosophy, ethics, media, and other cultural forms interpret, represent, and
respond to environmental change and ecological crisis. It considers how culture shapes public
understandings of nature, climate, development, technology, sustainability, and the relationship between
human and more-than-human worlds.

culture shapes public
understandings of nature, climate, development, technology, sustainability, and the relationship between
human and more-than-human worlds.
The course introduces major concepts and debates in the field, including ecocriticism, environmental
imagination, environmental justice, Anthropocene studies, posthumanism, new materialism, multispecies
studies, toxicity and waste, Blue Humanities, environmental memory, ecocinema, environmental media,
Indigenous ecological knowledge, climate fiction, and ecological futures. Students explore how stories,
images, archives, landscapes, and media practices reveal unequal environmental burdens, contested ideas
of progress, and the ethical challenges posed by climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, extraction,
and resource depletion.

Through global, Indian, and South Asian case studies, the course pays particular attention to the cultural
and political dimensions of environmental inequality, displacement, disaster, water, forests, coasts, urban
ecologies, and rural livelihoods. It examines how colonial histories, capitalism, caste, gender, class, race,
indigeneity, and geopolitics influence both environmental harm and possibilities for ecological care. By
bringing together critical theory with creative and cultural texts, students develop the tools to analyse
sustainability, justice, responsibility, resilience, and collective futures in an era of rapid planetary
transformation.

6. Course Description
This advanced doctoral-level course develops a theoretically rigorous and research-intensive
interdisciplinary framework for examining the entanglements between ecological degradation,
environmental change, illness, and planetary wellbeing across human and more-than-human worlds. It
approaches “ecosickness” as a critical and interpretive concept through which illness can be understood
not merely as an individual biomedical condition but as an embodied, ecological, cultural, political, and
planetary phenomenon. The course brings Environmental Humanities into sustained dialogue with
Planetary Health, Health Humanities, Medical Humanities, One Health, Political Ecology,
Environmental History, Posthumanism, New Materialism, Earth-system science, Science and
Technology Studies, and Critical Global Health.

alth, Political Ecology,
Environmental History, Posthumanism, New Materialism, Earth-system science, Science and
Technology Studies, and Critical Global Health.
A central intervention of the course is its interrogation of the historical separation between human health
and environmental health that has structured modernity, public health, medicine, development, and
environmental governance. It critically examines human exceptionalism, biomedical reductionism, and
the nature–culture divide, asking how the health of human bodies is inseparable from the health of
ecological systems. The course examines how climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, toxicity,
extractivism, altered disease ecologies, food and water insecurity, pandemics, urbanization, and
environmental disasters become embodied as illness, vulnerability, displacement, anxiety, grief, and
social suffering. Particular attention is given to the uneven distribution of environmental health risks
through caste, class, gender, indigeneity, disability, geography, coloniality, and political economy. The
course therefore asks not only who becomes sick under conditions of environmental change, but also
whose suffering becomes visible, whose knowledge counts, and how environmental futures are shaped
through unequal relations of power and expertise.

The course moves from the individual body to the social body, ecological body, and planetary body,
asking how bodies become sites where environmental histories are registered. Key concepts include
environmental health, planetary boundaries, the Anthropocene, the Great Acceleration, slow violence,
toxic embodiment, environmental illness, solastalgia, ecological grief, climate anxiety, ecological
distress, disaster trauma, environmental memory, multispecies health, transcorporeality, vulnerability,
resilience, and planetary justice. Students will critically examine ecological distress while resisting its
reduction to individual pathology and recognizing its social, ecological, and political dimensions.

Literary and cultural texts are central. Novels, short fiction, poetry, film, visual culture, testimony,
illness narratives, speculative fiction, ecocinema, and digital media will be read alongside scientific and
policy discourses. Primary and theoretical materials may include Amitav Ghosh, Margaret Atwood,
Richard Powers, Jeff VanderMeer, Kim Stanley Robinson, Paolo Bacigalupi, N. K. Jemisin, Indra
Sinha, Donna Haraway, Stacy Alaimo, Rob Nixon, Dipesh Chakrabarty, Ashlee Cunsolo, Glenn
Albrecht, Anna Tsing, Bruno Latour, Timothy Morton, Arturo Escobar, Achille Mbembe, and scholars
of Planetary Health Humanities. The course also engages Indigenous, feminist, decolonial, and more-
than-human perspectives on health, care, and ecological reciprocity.

At the advanced level, the course emphasizes conceptual synthesis, comparative analysis, close reading,
interdisciplinary research design, and critical engagement with competing epistemologies of health. It
culminates in the question of what it might mean to move from planetary illness toward planetary care,
ecological justice, regenerative futures, and a more expansive conception of “cosmogenic health.”

1. Critically examine the conceptual emergence of Planetary Health and its relationship to
Environmental Humanities, Health Humanities, Medical Humanities, One Health, and EcoHealth.

2. Develop a theoretically sophisticated understanding of “ecosickness” as a cultural, ecological,
embodied and planetary condition.

3. Interrogate the historical and philosophical separation of human health from environmental systems
and critically assess human exceptionalism and biomedical reductionism.

6. Analyse ecological grief, solastalgia, climate anxiety and environmental distress without

Course Description & Objectives:

Objectives

This course provides a rigorous, computational framework for quantifying the potential for future
shaking (Hazard) and the consequent financial or safety losses (Risk). This course bridges the gap
between Earth Science (source characterization) and Engineering (performance assessment).

In this course, students will use MATLAB to code the fundamental PSHA integrals and Risk
convolutions themselves, rather than relying on pre-packaged software.

The specific learning outcomes are:
1. Source & Ground Motion Characterization: Master the statistical fitting of earthquake
recurrence laws (Gutenberg-Richter) and the implementation of empirical Ground Motion
Models (GMMs) to predict intensity measures like PGA and Spectral Acceleration.

2. Computational DSHA and PSHA: Understand the difference between Deterministic
(Scenario-based) and Probabilistic (Rate-based) approaches, and learn when to apply each
(e.g., deterministic caps in design codes vs. risk-targeted design). Develop a custom
MATLAB solver to perform the PSHA integration, handling Aleatory Variability
(randomness in ground motion) and Epistemic Uncertainty (model uncertainty) via Logic
Trees.

3. Hazard De-aggregation & Selection: Identify "controlling earthquakes" through de-
aggregation and implement advanced ground motion selection algorithms (e.g., Conditional
Mean Spectrum) for engineering design.

Course Description
Sequence stratigraphy emerged as a paradigm shift in the discipline of stratigraphy. This emergent
branch of stratigraphy proved to be popular in industry and academia owing to its wide
applicability in energy exploration and in delivering analysis with a time-space reference. In
particular, contrary to the classical lithostratigraphic approach, sequence stratigraphy allows the
investigation with genetically-linked, hiatus-bounded strata in a chronostratigraphic framework.
Broadly, in this course, the students will learn various concepts and tools of sequence stratigraphy
that will help their academic preparation and professional career. This course will focus on aspects
of: terminology and methods of sequence stratigraphy, and their application to subsurface
reservoirs; concepts of hierarchy of stratigraphic architecture at various scales (from parasequence
to systems tracts to sequence); criteria-based interpretation and recognition of sequence
stratigraphic surfaces in outcrops, subsurface core-cuttings, wireline logs, and seismic sections;
comprehension on similarities and dissimilarities among several sequence stratigraphic models
(depositional sequence stratigraphy, transgressive-regressive sequence stratigraphy, genetic
sequence stratigraphy, etc.), on analysis of clastic vs. non-clastic (carbonate) sequence
stratigraphy; use of (nearby) field locations for field training of various concepts. Overall, this
course will help the students how to think and communicate like a sequence stratigrapher within
the wider context of sedimentary geology.

Course Description

Successful reservoir analysis is critically linked to optimal exploration, production and management
of natural resources (oil, gas, coal, water), and associated approaches (e.g., environmental measures);
it therefore influences societal and economic prosperity at national and international scales. This
course will help students gain a sound understanding of various concepts and tools for reservoir
characterization at multiple scales: from pore to basin. Teaching topics will focus on: formation
mechanism of seal, reservoir and source rocks, emplacement of these rock types in various traps (e.g.,
stratigraphic vs. structural); Reservoir conditioning mechanisms at different settings (fluvial, eolian,
shallow water, deep water) and environments (clastic; non-clastic: carbonate); Use of data types
(outcrop, core, well-log, GPR, seismic) and tools (e.g., lithostratigraphy, biostratigraphy, sequence
stratigraphy) for reservoir prediction; how effects of pore-scale to meso-scale to macro-scale features
constrain reservoir heterogeneity and associated risks (e.g., variability in reservoir

ediction; how effects of pore-scale to meso-scale to macro-scale features
constrain reservoir heterogeneity and associated risks (e.g., variability in reservoir properties such as
porosity and permeability); syn-depositional and post-depositional (e.g., fractures, joints) effects on
reservoir compartmentalization and drainage. Students will get to know how to use multi-dimensional
datasets to evaluate: reservoir attributes (e.g., thickness, area, drainage, net-to-gross); facies- to
architecture- to geobody-scale reservoir complexity by analyzing (1) lithologs (2) Bioturbation Index
(BI) logs, and (3) object-based and process-based models. With use of case studies, students will
comprehend reservoir characterization in conventional vs. unconventional (e.g., tight gas) systems,
in energy sectors (oil, gas, coal), in water management (aquifer analysis), in new energy frontiers
(e.g., geothermal), and in emerging scientific thrust areas such as geologic carbon sequestration.

subject to safety requirements. It connects constrained Markov decision processes with robust
reachability, control barrier functions, and optimization-based safety filters. Students will learn to

incorporate model uncertainty into controller design. The course also introduces conformal prediction and
conformal risk control for statistical calibration of uncertainty and risk. Analytical exercises and
computational case studies will develop students’ ability to evaluate the assumptions, guarantees, and
performance limitations of safe learning methods.

Course description:
a. Objectives: Machine-learning components are increasingly being deployed in safety-critical and
high-stakes systems, creating new challenges for verification and testing. Unlike conventional
software, learned models are often not derived from explicit, human-written specifications, and
their behavior depends on data, training procedures, and complex model architectures.
Consequently, traditional verification and testing approaches must be adapted and extended to
provide meaningful assurance of AI-based systems.
This course aims to equip students with the principles and techniques needed to systematically
verify and test AI-based systems and assess their readiness for deployment. Students will learn
to formulate testable requirements and formal properties for machine-learning components; test
datasets and deep neural networks using white-box and black-box techniques while efficiently
prioritizing tests under limited labeling budgets; and evaluate properties such as robustness,
uncertainty, and fairness. The course will also cover formal verification of neural networks,
including quantized networks, as well as verification and testing of systems incorporating neural
components. For closed-loop and autonomous systems, students will study reachability analysis,
falsification, scenario-based testing, and runtime assurance to establish safety and reliability
under diverse operating conditions.

6. Course Description:

A) Objectives:
This course introduces students to artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and scientific machine
learning techniques for weather and climate modelling and prediction. Students will gain foundational knowledge
of atmospheric processes, climate datasets, Earth system modelling and numerical weather prediction. The course
covers classical machine learning methods, deep learning architectures, graph-based learning, neural operators,
and emerging foundation models for weather forecasting. Students will learn to analyze observational, reanalysis,
and climate datasets, develop data-driven forecasting models, evaluate modern AI-based forecasting systems and
gain hands-on experience with state-of-the-art tools for weather forecasting, and Earth-system modeling.

8. Course Description: This course develops a complete pipeline from climate science to
quantifying risk and decision-making for a warming world, integrating physics (theory),
machine learning (AI), and real-world applications. Students learn about the climate system
and sustainability framing, then progress through understanding climate modeling and using
climate models, including data assimilation and parameterizations using machine learning,
designing surrogates and emulators with rigorous uncertainty quantification, downscaling
climate extremes that resolve tails for estimating risk, and linking climate scenarios to
specific locations. Quantifying risk as the product of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability, they
learn to map exposure using computer vision and remote sensing, quantify vulnerability
with structured methods and large language model tools, and translate risk metrics into
actionable insights using stochastic dynamic programming, reinforcement learning, and
serious games. Every topic is anchored in a single case study and specific methods so that
the concepts accumulate into an end-to-end workflow. The class is structured to include
short preparatory materials, such as tutorials or recorded walkthroughs, made available
before class. Guest speakers may be included from time to time to connect students to
operating centers and agencies. In addition to regular assignments and exams, the course
may comprise a capstone project that presents an integrated, defensible plan for addressing
climate risk and resilience, ultimately leading to sustainable outcomes.

9. Objectives: On completing this course, students will be able to:

● Understand the foundations of climate and sustainability: explain the climate system, its
feedbacks, and its connections to sustainability and resilience.

● Operate and augment climate models by running baseline models, applying data
assimilation, and utilizing machine learning for parameterization and calibration.

● Construct AI- and physics-coupled surrogates, quantify uncertainty and extremes, and
downscale climate fields to local scales.

● Quantify and communicate climate risk by integrating hazard, exposure, and vulnerability to
compute risk portfolios, and clearly communicate uncertainty and trade-offs.

● Design sustainable decisions for resilience using physics and learning: apply optimization,
reinforcement learning, and serious games to evaluate adaptation and mitigation strategies
in key sectors (FEWS, coastal, and urban systems).

B) Content

1. Introduction to Climate and Sustainability (2 Lectures): Overview of Earth’s energy and
water cycles, circulation, and feedbacks. Introduce climate sensitivity, including radiative
forcing and the role of feedbacks in determining Earth’s response to greenhouse gases. Links
to human systems, SDGs, equity, and institutions. Natural Step, Natural Capital,
Precautionary Principles, planetary boundaries, socio-ecological systems, and ecosystem
services accounting. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) fundamentals with limitations and
uncertainty.
2. What is Climate Resilience (2): Weather vs climate, predictability scales, climate as a
distribution; nonstationarity; extremes and risk. IPCC scenarios and CMIP6 models.
Adaptation and mitigation portfolios, resilience planning. The integrated cycle of projecting
climate forward and backcasting decisions based on time-evolving risk; the key role of AI
across the loop.

The aim of this course is to introduce the concepts of behavioral economics to management
students and management practitioners. Economic thought has advanced in recent decades
beyond the traditional microeconomic theories that assume rational behavior and are based on

that emerge from such departures. This course is not mathematical and will instead focus on
some of the outcomes of new ways of understanding human behavior. I will require reading of

Course description: Public debates on important economic issues are often shaped by conven-
tional wisdom. This course examines a set of widely debated economic issues through the lens of
economic concepts and empirical evidence. It begins by exploring why and how conventional wis-
dom shapes public discourse on economic issues, and then applies economic reasoning and empirical
evidence to a set of topics including migration, international trade, economic growth, taxation, au-
tomation, minimum wages, and the role of government. The course aims to develop the ability to
critically assess competing claims about economic issues using reasoned and evidence-based argu-
ments. Rather than providing simple answers, the course emphasizes trade-offs, historical context,
and the strengths and limitations of alternative approaches in evaluating the critical issues facing
societies and economies.

• Marketing 1.0 (Product-Centric): Focused on industrial production, functionality, and mass
marketing. The goal was to sell products, often with one-way communication.
• Marketing 2.0 (Consumer-Centric): Shifted to segmenting markets and understanding consumer
needs. Emphasized loyalty, bidirectional communication, and emotional connection.
• Marketing 3.0 (Values-Driven): Recognized customers as whole human beings with minds,
hearts, and spirits. Focused on corporate social responsibility and making the world better.
• Marketing 4.0 (Digital Transformation): Merged traditional and digital marketing (moving
from 4P to 4C). Focused on personalization, big data, and high-tech/high-touch interactions.
• Marketing 5.0 (Human-Centric Technology): Leveraged AI, IoT, and automated technology to
create personalized customer experiences, aiming to augment human marketers.
• Marketing 6.0 (Immersive "Phygital"): Blurs the lines between digital and physical worlds.

6. Course Description: Elective for Ph.D., Masters, and senior UG students in mechanical engineering, and other

r UG students in mechanical engineering, and other

(A) Objectives:
Real elastic solids are rarely perfectly homogeneous. Their mass density, elastic moduli, microstructure, geometry,
defects, and interfaces exhibit spatial variability. When this variability is modeled probabilistically, the equations
of elasticity become stochastic, leading to a mechanics of random elastic media. Such models arise in composites,
porous and heterogeneous materials, polycrystals, metamaterials, granular media, damaged solids, and materials
with uncertain microstructure.

• To introduce the role of randomness and uncertainty in mechanical systems and to distinguish deterministic
mechanics from stochastic mechanics and random-media models.

• To introduce random mechanical structures, including random walks, graphs, lattices, point processes, random
fields, random tensors, random matrices, and random interfaces.

random mechanical structures, including random walks, graphs, lattices, point processes, random
fields, random tensors, random matrices, and random interfaces.
• To connect microscopic structural randomness and material heterogeneity with macroscopic mechanical response
through equilibrium, wave propagation, homogenization, instability, fracture, and reliability concepts.

• To introduce computational and data-driven tools for stochastic mechanics, including Monte Carlo simulation,
random-field representations, and physics-informed/data-driven modelling.

The proposed course develops mechanics starting from the equations of elasticity and uses random media as the
central theme. This connects probability with elastic equilibrium, wave propagation, homogenization, effective
constitutive laws, scattering, localization, and computational mechanics.

6. Course description
A) Objectives:
ME621 is a compulsory foundational course for incoming graduate students in solid mechanics and for the
proposed postgraduate programme in computational mechanics. The course develops an understanding of
deformation, stress, balance laws, constitutive behaviour, and the formulation of boundary-value problems. It
prepares students to approach unfamiliar problems with sound mechanical reasoning and to pursue advanced
study in solid and computational mechanics. The course aims to cultivate an appreciation of the subject
through careful examination of assumptions, physical interpretation, and the limits of models.
Linear isotropic elasticity provides the main working framework. Selected analytical solutions illustrate the
structure of the theory and provide benchmarks for checking predictions. Thermoelasticity and linear
viscoelasticity extend this foundation through thermal eigenstrain and material memory. An expository field-
coupling module introduces magnetoelasticity, with emphasis on formulating a new problem using familiar
principles.

B) Course outline:
The course comprises 40 lectures of 50 minutes each. Every module ends with one supervised in-class
problem-solving session (of around 30-50 minutes). In the following, a brief description of contents in each
module is followed by suggestions (in smaller font) for the supervised problem-solving session. The instructor
can choose a problem from the suggestions according to her/his taste.
Module 1 Deformation and compatibility (5 lectures)
Tensor notation and calculus through mechanical examples; reference and deformed configurations;
deformation gradient; finite and infinitesimal strain; physical interpretation; principal strains; compatibility.
Use an affine displacement field to identify normal and shear strains, principal directions, and changes of lengths and angles.
Compare an infinitesimal rotation with a finite rigid rotation to expose the limits of linearised strain. Give a simple planar strain
field and ask whether it is compatible and whether a displacement can be recovered locally. Discuss the role of domain topology
when interpreting local compatibility.
Module 2 Stress and balance laws (4 lectures)
Traction and Cauchy stress; interpretation and principal stresses; linear and angular momentum balances;
assumptions behind stress symmetry; equilibrium and the role of inertia.
For a given stress tensor, determine traction on differently oriented planes and interpret normal and shear components. Use a
polynomial stress field to test equilibrium and infer required body forces. Check the global force and moment balance of
boundary tractions. Ask what assumptions permit a symmetric Cauchy stress and when neglect of inertia is appropriate.

[PAGE 2]
Module 3 Constitutive modelling (4 lectures)
Isotropic linear elasticity; elastic constants; stress power and stored energy; positive definiteness; Mechanical
work, heat, and internal energy; distinction between energy conservation and dissipation; entropy and
Helmholtz free energy at an introductory level. Constitutive potentials and their role in elastic and coupled
material response.
Compare uniaxial stress with uniaxial strain in the same isotropic material. Separate volumetric and distortional responses and
examine positive strain energy and admissible elastic constants. Use loading and unloading paths to distinguish elastic storage
from dissipation.
Module 4 Formulating an elastic problem (5 lectures)
Strong formulation and Navier equations; displacement and traction boundary conditions; virtual work and
weak formulation; rigid-body modes; uniqueness and superposition.
Formulate an elastic body with mixed boundary conditions and identify missing supports, rigid-body motions, or unbalanced
prescribed tractions. Derive the weak form of an axially loaded bar and then

oundary conditions and identify missing supports, rigid-body motions, or unbalanced
prescribed tractions. Derive the weak form of an axially loaded bar and then extend the reasoning to a small-strain solid.
Illustrate the usefulness of uniqueness and superposition using a simple problem.
Module 5 Reductions and selected exact solutions (4 lectures)
Plane stress, plane strain, anti-plane shear and axisymmetry; validity of reductions; selected cylinder problems.
Use a pressurised thick cylinder to compare plane-strain and free-end or closed-end idealisations. Consider simple plane
problems and illustrate their validity with respect to the full 3-D problem. Ask students to check assumptions and boundary
conditions before evaluating stresses.
Module 6 Stress concentrations and singularities (5 lectures)
Circular-hole fields; stress concentration; singular wedge problems; physical interpretation of singularities.
Supply selected expressions for stresses around a circular hole and ask students to check traction-free conditions, far-field
behaviour, and stress concentration. Compare a

Module 7 Thermoelasticity (4 lectures)
Thermal eigenstrain, free-expansion and constraints, compatibility and residual stress, all with prescribed
temperature fields; heat conduction and an introduction to coupled thermal-mechanical formulations.
Revisit an elastic bar under uniform heating, first with free ends and then with fixed ends or an elastic support. Extend the
example to a bonded pair with different thermal expansion coefficients. Ask when thermal eigenstrain can be accommodated
without stress; spatial variation alone is insufficient to establish that stress must occur. Formulate a simple steady conduction
problem and distinguish a prescribed temperature field from a coupled thermal-mechanical calculation.

Apply a step strain or step stress to a standard linear solid. Sketch the response before solving, identify the correct initial

Magnetoelastic modelling using a supplied consistent constitutive potential; magnetic field variables and

management systems for electronics, such as heat sinks, heat pipes/thermosiphons/vapor
chambers, microchannel heat exchangers, and thermoelectric devices. The course will also
cover hardware for thermal management of various electronic systems, including consumer
electronics, defence, and space applications. Upon completion of this course, students will
be able to analyze and design thermal management solutions for electronic systems. This
course will present students with practical and theoretical problems that will help them
develop the quantitative skills required to model, evaluate, and optimize heat transfer in
electronic devices and systems.

emerging technology trends.
• Identify the electrical, thermal, and mechanical factors governing semiconductor
package performance.
• Analyze the effects of material properties, thermal expansion mismatch, and
thermomechanical stresses on package reliability.

and predicting solder joint fatigue life.
• Apply statistical methods, including Weibull analysis and lifetime distributions, to
interpret reliability data and estimate component lifetime.
• Evaluate design challenges and reliability considerations in advanced packaging
technologies, including 2.5D/3D integration, chiplets, and hybrid bonding.

• Course Description:

This is an introductory number theory course with a focus on quadratic fields. The main goal is
to study the prime ideals and the units in the ring of integers of quadratic fields. In particular, we
will explore the relation of the ideal class group of imaginary quadratic fields with the binary
quadratic forms and also with the (Dedekind) Zeta function via the class number formula. We
will also study quadratic reciprocity, and the Brahmagupta-Pell's equation. The course will be
largely self contained and necessary tools from algebra and analysis will be developed along the
way in the course.

Course Objective
This course develops stochastic analysis as a mathematical method for studying local and nonlocal partial differential
equations. Probability, martingales, Brownian motion, Itô integration and SDEs provide the foundations for diffusion gen-
erators, stopped processes, Dynkin’s formula, Kolmogorov equations and Feynman–Kac representations. An introductory
treatment of Lévy processes connects jump generators to integro-differential equations and the fractional Laplacian. The
emphasis is on precise regularity and integrability hypotheses, selected proofs, and stochastic representations of initial
and boundary/exterior value problems.

Course Objective

This is an advanced course on the regularity theory of elliptic partial diﬀerential equations. The
course develops the principal analytical techniques used to obtain qualitative and quantitative
regularity estimates for weak and viscosity solutions.

The course begins with a review of Sobolev spaces, weak derivatives, weak solutions, and funda-
mental inequalities, followed by the study of H2-regularity for elliptic equations. The classical
Schauder theory is then introduced, providing regularity estimates in H¨older spaces.

7. Overview of the Course: This course provides an introduction to the numerical analy-
sis of first-order hyperbolic PDEs. We begin with linear hyperbolic equations and develop
numerical methods based on finite difference approximations. We study the fundamental
concepts of consistency, stability, and convergence of these methods. We then turn to scalar
nonlinear conservation laws. Starting with the method of characteristics, we analyze shock
formation, derive the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions, study rarefaction waves, and discuss the
theory of weak and entropy solutions. The course then focuses on finite volume methods for
scalar conservation laws. We study first-order schemes, including the Godunov method and
monotone schemes, and examine the concepts of consistency, conservation, and monotonicity
together with their stability and convergence properties. We then move to high-resolution
finite volume methods, including Lax–Wendroff, TVD, MUSCL, and WENO schemes. Time
integration techniques will be discussed, with emphasis on Strong Stability Preserving (SSP)
properties. Finally, we extend these ideas to linear and nonlinear systems of hyperbolic con-
servation laws. Applications include linear systems such as the linear acoustics equations and
nonlinear systems such as the shallow water equations and the Euler equations.

course, students will gain hands-on experience by implementing these numerical methods in
MATLAB or Python, as well as in the Clawpack software that is used to simulate complex
physical phenomena such as water waves and fluid flow.

8. Course Description:
Indian Logic (in Sanskrit anviksiki, nyaya, or tarka) is the tradition of systematic reasoning of the
Indian subcontinent, evolved over nearly two millennia from roughly the sixth century BCE onward. It
is distinctive in that it examines not only the forms of acceptable arguments, but also the sources of
valid cognition (pramanas), namely perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony. Hence
logic, epistemology and language are viewed as one continuous study. Validity is analyzed in
connection with justified belief and reliable sources (including testimony, a category that Western
analytic philosophy has only recently considered respectable). The tradition matured in public

nd reliable sources (including testimony, a category that Western
analytic philosophy has only recently considered respectable). The tradition matured in public
deliberative assemblies with formalized rules of debate, and it produced a rich technical apparatus:
the five-membered syllogism of the Nyaya school, the three-condition doctrine of the Buddhist
logicians, the sevenfold predication of Jainism (saptabhangi), sophisticated theories of truth and
error, a precise taxonomy of fallacies (hetvabhasa), and even explicitly non-classical, many-valued
modes of reasoning such as the Buddhist four-cornered analysis (catuskoti). This course aims to
provide students with the skills to understand, systemize, evaluate, and compare the primary Indian
logical frameworks, while recognizing their continued importance in contemporary intellectual
debate.

be compared with Western logic.

C) Short summary for including in the Courses of Study Booklet:
Indian logic (known in Sanskrit as anviksiki, nyāya, or tarka) is a tradition of systematic reasoning that
emerged in the Indian subcontinent and evolved over roughly two millennia, beginning around the
sixth century BCE. This course introduces Indian traditions of logic and reasoning. The course surveys
key schools—Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, Advaita Vedānta, Cārvāka,
Jainism, and Buddhist logic—emphasizing theories of knowledge (pramāṇa), inference (anumāna),
perception (pratyakṣa), testimony (śabda), and negation (abhāva). No prior background in philosophy,
Sanskrit, or logic is required. How do we come to know what we know, and what makes an argument
sound? It addresses both questions by exploring India’s rigorous traditions of inquiry, ranging from
the Cārvāka skeptics and the realist logicians of Nyāya to the Buddhist epistemologists and the Jain
philosophers who embrace many‑valued truth, and by engaging them in a careful dialogue with

list logicians of Nyāya to the Buddhist epistemologists and the Jain
philosophers who embrace many‑valued truth, and by engaging them in a careful dialogue with
[PAGE 4]
modern symbolic logic. The course culminates in a balanced assessment of five questions: Where do
Indian traditions resemble classical logic? Which are better compared with epistemic, modal, many-
valued, or defeasible frameworks? Why is Jaina syādvāda not simply many-valued logic? Is Indian
logic "epistemic logic"? And how do pramā-based accounts of knowledge compare with Plato's and
with the modern justified-true-belief model?

economic perspective, focusing on how resources are allocated, priced, and governed to meet
growing energy needs under environmental and sustainability constraints. It explains the
drivers of energy demand and supply, evaluates energy investments using standard financial
and economic criteria, and assesses the functioning of energy markets. Students will also gain
the ability to interpret energy data, apply decomposition and elasticity concepts, and utilize
modeling frameworks to analyze future energy scenarios and transition pathways. Overall, the
course will equip them with the capacity to critically evaluate alternative energy strategies and
support evidence-based decision-making in the context of climate change and low-carbon

Course Objectives
This course provides an integrated understanding of how structure, interfaces, and phase stability
govern the behaviour of modern functional materials used in energy applications. Comparing and
contrasting traditional metallurgy-centric treatments, the course emphasizes multiphase,
heterogeneous, and composite systems, where interfaces and defects play a critical role in enabling
functionality. Students will develop a rigorous foundation in crystallography, diffraction, and defects,
alongside thermodynamics, phase equilibria, and transformation kinetics, and learn to interpret phase
diagrams in the context of both equilibrium and processing-driven (metastable) materials. Special
emphasis is placed on distinguishing classical mixtures from engineered composites, and on
understanding how structural complexity and interfacial phenomena influence performance in
systems such as photovoltaics, batteries, fuel cells, and catalytic materials.

ding how structural complexity and interfacial phenomena influence performance in
systems such as photovoltaics, batteries, fuel cells, and catalytic materials.
Expected Learning Outcomes
Students will be able to analyze and describe the crystal structure and phase constitution of
functional materials. They will develop the ability to apply thermodynamic principles and phase
diagrams to assess phase stability under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. Students will
understand the critical role of defects, interfaces, and heterogeneous architectures in governing
transport, reactivity, and device performance. They will also distinguish between classical mixtures
and engineered composites, and evaluate how processing and kinetics influence their formation and
stability. Finally, students will be equipped to connect fundamental materials concepts to practical
applications in energy and electronic systems.

6. Course Description: This course builds the foundation for understanding energy systems and
the low-carbon transition. It equips students to analyze the energy demand using elasticity and
decomposition methods, appraise supply investments through NPV, LCOE, and Marginal
Abatement Cost analysis, and evaluate policy instruments, carbon pricing, CBAM, fiscal
incentives, and just transition measures using welfare and externality frameworks. Energy
modelling tools including LEAP, TIMES-MARKAL, and LCA are applied to construct and
interpret India-specific transition scenarios. By the end, students will be equipped to critically
evaluate alternative energy strategies, identify efficiency-equity trade-offs in policy design,
and formulate evidence-based recommendations for low-carbon development under market
and policy uncertainty.

to understand not just how energy systems work, but why they are structured the way they are,
where they fail, and what interventions can correct them. Equally, the course seeks to cultivate
critical engagement with energy modelling and policy design, ensuring students to interrogate
the assumptions behind scenarios and recommendations.

D) Short summary for including in the course of study booklet: This course aims to
develop an understanding of digital finance with human society at its core. Specifically, the
course approaches digital finance from the perspective of it’s consumers. Both the promises
and challenges of digital finance as an important social intervention are examined here.
Through the examination of real-world cases across the globe, it will develop an
understanding that the outcomes of interventions through digital finance emerge through
an interaction between rapidly evolving financial technology, regulatory-legal
arrangements, social structures, and human agency (exerted both at the collective and
individual level). While top-down, macro perspectives of digital finance are well
understood, this course aims to train students in enhancing how it operates at the micro and
meso levels in society. In light of this, the course will examine how varying populations
engage with the diverse instruments of digital finance as part of their routine social lives.
Consequently, students will be trained to examine how social factors that shape how
households and communities engage with digital finance as part of their interactions with
other. They will also receive training in understanding how social arrangements shape the
use of digital finance in gift-giving, savings and investment and debt. Finally, the course
will introduce students to sustainable approaches to digital finance through a historical-
comparative analysis of instruments and interventions over time.

6. Course Description
A) Objectives
Energy infrastructure systems and AI-based digital systems are undergoing large-scale transformation.
These transitions change how work is organised, how institutions function, and how communities
sustain livelihoods. Sociology studies how such large technical systems reshape social relations,
labour arrangements, and everyday life. This course examines these changes through the concept of
just transition.

Engineers and technology managers increasingly make decisions that extend beyond technical
performance. Site selection, system architecture, automation level, data use, labour arrangements, and
user access conditions all influence project viability. Projects can fail not because the technology does
not work, but because social, institutional, or regulatory conditions were not anticipated during
planning.

This course introduces students to methods for analysing technology deployment in real operating
environments. Using cases from India and international contexts, students will examine how energy
infrastructure, digital platforms, and AI systems interact with labour markets, local economies, and
governance frameworks. The course connects technical decisions to practical constraints such as land
acquisition, workforce transition, compliance requirements, and reputational risk.

[PAGE 2]
Students will learn to:
• identify stakeholders affected by technology deployment
• analyse distribution of costs, benefits, and risks
• understand how regulation and institutional structure affect engineering choices
• evaluate trade-offs between efficiency, reliability, and social impact
• prepare structured deployment analyses for real-world applications

The course uses examples including coal region transition, renewable energy siting, platform work,
and AI-enabled services. No prior background in social science is required.

D) Short Summary for Courses of Study Booklet
Just Transition: An Inclusive Pathway to Energy and AI Technologies (SOC XXX).
The energy transition and the AI revolution are changing economies, labour markets, and communities
at a pace and scale not seen before. Both transitions produce winners and losers. The losers are often
those who are already at the margins of economy and society. This course asks: how do technology
transitions interact with structural inequalities of class, caste, gender, and region, and what can
technology leaders do about it? Using sociology, economics, policy analysis, and data from India and
the world, students learn to see what is often hidden: the coal worker, the data annotator, the displaced
community, and the platform worker managed by an algorithm. India is the primary case. International
cases include Germany, South Africa, the EU, and the United States. The course is designed for
students who will lead technology companies, shape national AI and energy policy, and contribute to
global technology governance. The course treats energy networks and AI platforms as social systems
that organise labour, risk, and access to resources. No prerequisites. Open to all branches from the
second year.

The course offers a socio-legal perspective on the transformation of the institutions of family,
kinship and marriage. As these traditional social institutions transmute into their modern
avatar, the nature of this transformation calls for sociological unpacking. Here, two distinct sets
of normative frames operate in collocation—societal and legal. This leads to a contestation that
Emile Durkheim had identified as anomie, a hallmark of all societies transitioning from status
to contract. Taking a comparative lens, the course traces these changes in India since the
colonial period. We undertake this exercise by analyzing the legal developments in the domain
of family and kinship from the nineteenth century to the present. This broad overview will
equip the students to appreciate the importance and impact of legislative changes on family
and kinship. At the same time, the course will delve into a detailed analysis of specific reforms—
marriage, divorce and succession acts—to understand how the religion-based family law system
works in India and its broader societal impacts, including the economy. The effect of family
law reform on gender will be discussed in detail. This course will help students understand how
family and kinship are affected by recent legal changes (the Uniform Civil Code, amendments
to the Succession Act, the Senior Citizen Act, among others) and their future directions.

Human-centered computing(HCC) studies
computing systems that are designed to support
human activity. For example, search engines
support information search, e-commerce supports
economic consumption; increasingly, computing
systems are also taking over managerial and
organizational roles in service-sharing ecosystems.
At the core of all such systems lie assumptions
about the needs and expectations of humans, their
eventual design is meant to facilitate these
expectations. How specifically should a natural
language search query be interpreted, based on a
user’s past search history? How diverse should a
music playlist recommendation be, based on the
current pattern of song choices of the user? The
academic discipline of HCC studies such questions
in the bigger theoretical structure of a two-way
interaction between agent expectations and system
design: systematizing various elements of

dies such questions
in the bigger theoretical structure of a two-way
interaction between agent expectations and system
design: systematizing various elements of human
behavior that can be reliably measured by
computing systems; and determining how best to
design computing systems that can adaptively
interact with such behavioral elements.

Thus, there is a dire need for automated malware
analysis systems which produce effective results
with minimal human intervention. Antivirus systems
use the most common and primitive approach,
which involves the generation of signatures of
known malware beforehand and then comparing
newly downloaded executables against these
signatures to predict its nature. This technique
drastically fails in case of any zero-day malware, a
malware which has been newly created and thus a
signature is not available. Other common
techniques are static analysis and dynamic analysis.
Static analysis analyzes the executables without
executing it and predicts the results. It is generally
used because it’s relatively fast but fails if the
malware is packed, encrypted or obfuscated. To
overcome the limitations of static approaches
another approach, i.e., dynamic analysis is used. It
involves collecting behavioural data by executing
the sample in a sandboxed environment and then
using it for detection and classification. The dynamic
analysis also has some limitations such as the
detection of virtual environment and code coverage
issues. As a result, researchers have started using
the combination of both the approaches known as a
hybrid approach.

Memory subsystem is an important layer in the
computing system that has to be efficient for the
whole system to operate efficiently. In the current
era of computation, multiple cores are deployed in
devices that range from smart-phones, laptops,
desktops, servers, and cloud based systems.

computer architecture have resulted in faster

in the form of side-channel and covert-channel
attacks (for example, the recent meltdown and

The course deals with applications of Markov chains
techniques in certain areas of computer
science and of biology. The unifying aspect in these
applications is the role played by mixing
time analysis, which is the focus of the course.
In a typical combinatorial optimization problem, each
instance x is associated with a state
space Sx, usually of size exponential in the size of
x, where each element of Sx has an
associated cost (or a value). The problem is to nd a
state with minimum cost (or with
maximum value). In the Markov chains approach to
solving such a problem, a Markov
chain is associated with each instance with the
property that the goal state has the highest
probability in the stationary distribution of the chain.
Success of this approach crucially
depends on the mixing time of the associated chain,
that is, how quickly does the chain
come close to its stationary distribution.
Markov chains have also been used to model
evolution for the nite population case lending
themseves to stochastic e ects. For a population of
size N of m types, a state of the chain
is the labelling of the N individuals each into one of

The result of the evolution modelled by the chain is
given by the stationary distribution
of the chain. In most cases however, it is not known
how to determine the stationary
distribution directly, we need to simulate the chain

the resulting distribution to obtain statistical
properties of the distribution. We need to
determine the mixing time of the chain to nd out how

been established recently that the expected motion
of such evolutionary chains turns out
to be a dynamical system, the trajectory of which
determines the mixing time properties
like rapid mixing.

To what degree functions of the mind can be
reproduced or simulated by a computer is a question
that has become volubly prominent in recent years.
It is often posed for public consumption as a matter
of ends – when will computer performance surpass
human performance on interesting challenges. From
a scientific standpoint, it is more useful to ask this
Computational CognitiveCS786 question from the standpoint of means – Science
what resources do organisms have available that let
them respond adaptively to situations they
encounter in the world?

This is the question that computational cognitive
scientists seek to answer. Such research frequently
starts from parametric characterizations of empirical

ld?

This is the question that computational cognitive
scientists seek to answer. Such research frequently
starts from parametric characterizations of empirical
[PAGE 107]
behavior. Theorists then develop computational
models that capture the quantitative relationship
between these parameters and various
experimental conditions. A good empirical fit permits
further questions of biological and epistemic
plausibility to be asked of the model. Models that
pass these quasi-philosophical checks graduate to
the status of theories. These accounts are,
inevitably, challenged as incomplete or erroneous
by further iterations of experiments and models.

The cycle of research in cognitive science,
therefore, encompasses, in order of the workflow
presented above, neuroscience and psychology,
statistics, computer science, and philosophy. This
course is meant to give both UG and PG students
interested in the computational aspects of cognitive
science a relatively comprehensive overview of the
discipline.

Course Description:
Current machine learning algorithms often deal with
datasets having hundred or thousands of features.
In the unsupervised learning setting, often such
datasets are modelled as random samples from a
highdimensional distribution which we are
interested to learn. Bayesian Networks are a
popular class of probabilistic graphical model that
allows us to succinctly represent high-dimensional
probability distributions owing to a limited
conditional dependence between the component
random variables. These networks have been used
to model large datasets across several practical
topics including Bioinfomatics, Medical Diagnosis,
Information Retrieval, Image Processing. In this
Algorithms For Bayesian
CS798D course, we take up a formal algorithmic study of
Networks And Causality
Bayesian networks. We will look at the central
problem of efficiently learning an unknown Bayesian
network using an optimal number of samples. Along
the way, we will touch upon several information-
theoretic tools which are useful in data science.

In the second part of the course, we will study
Causality using graphical models. Here we
consider the probabilistic dependence of each node
in the Bayesian network as an independent
mechanism subject to manipulation. Specifically,
the causal effect of a set of nodes on another is
formalized by an intervention that fixes a set of
nodes of the Bayes net to particular values ignoring
their parents while all other nodes are still governed
by the usual probabilistic dependence of the Bayes
net. We will discuss several important problems that
includes learning causal effects and causal models
from observational and interventional data.

Objective
Over the last few years, program analysis
techniques have been applied to a variety of
systems. Many of these cannot be perceived as
“conventional” sequential programs written in
languages like C, Python or Java. For example,
there have been attempts at testing and verifying
network routing policies, machine language models,
database schemas, concurrent systems,
probabilistic/randomized systems and
hardware/software co-designs. This course will
explore how program analysis techniques have
been adapted for such “unconventional” programs.

semantics, type systems;
Program Analysis of Sequential Programs: control-
flow and dataflow analysis, abstract interpretation,
deductive verification, fuzzing, symbolic execution;
Analysis of concurrent systems: memory
consistency models, duductive techniques (like
Owicki-Gries), vector-clock based dynamic
techniques;

What Is The Course About?
Daily we come across several computing devices
and tools (from smartwatch trackers to search
engines). Some of them are a delight to use, and
some are crappy and frustrating to learn,
Human-Computer understand and use – ever wondered what makesCS798H 3-0-0-0 (9)
Interaction them so? Ever wondered why using a smartphone
or learning to code so easy and natural for some
people, and so hard for others? Is digital
transformation in India going to take off, or no, and
why? All these, and more, are the concerns of
Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) as a field.

[PAGE 113]
In this course, we will cover the basic ground for
HCI, considering how we can study how people
interact with computers (if any) in a given context,
how to identify opportunities for improvements to
their work, and how to systematically design
systems that are a delight.
The field itself is interdisciplinary and borrows
theories and methods from various fields including
psychology, computer science, design, sociology
and anthropology. This course will give a flavor of
this interdisciplinary nature, as well as introduce you
to these methods and theories that will come in
handy in a lot of contexts. We will also consider
some common contexts in which Human-Computer
interaction is tricky, what we can do about it, and
where the open problems lie!

Mathematics and Statistics Course Rationale: The
early pioneers of the Internet envisioned it would be
the great equalizer and lead to the complete
democratization of the online world—nearly four
decades since the reality has diverged considerably
from their grand vision. Rather than the bastion of
freedom and free speech, which the early
visionaries envisioned, the Internet has become a
dangerous place. Data theft leading to identity theft
has become commonplace. Despite these
challenges, it is undeniable that the Internet has
revolutionized our lives by making day-to-day tasks
easier and connecting people worldwide —
however, the risks associated with the Internet loom
large. Secure Computation is a promising technique
that allows users to keep their data private without
sacrificing the Internet's benefits. Interestingly, the
origins of Secure Computation were during the
exact times when the Internet was in its nascent
stages. The early researchers of Secure
Computation studied it mainly as a theoretical
endeavor. However, nearly four decades after its
inception, Secure Computation is more than just a
problem of theoretical importance; it can solve
practical privacy problems many of which arise due
to the expansion of the Internet.

Human-centered computing(HCC) studies
computing systems that are designed to support
human activity. For example, search engines
support information search, e-commerce supports
economic consumption; increasingly, computing
systems are also taking over managerial and
organizational roles in service-sharing ecosystems.
At the core of all such systems lie assumptions
about the needs and expectations of humans, their
eventual design is meant to facilitate these
expectations. How specifically should a natural
language search query be interpreted, based on a
user’s past search history? How diverse should a
music playlist recommendation be, based on the
current pattern of song choices of the user? The
academic discipline of HCC studies such questions
in the bigger theoretical structure of a two-way
interaction between agent expectations and system
design: systematizing various elements of

dies such questions
in the bigger theoretical structure of a two-way
interaction between agent expectations and system
design: systematizing various elements of human
behavior that can be reliably measured by
computing systems; and determining how best to
design computing systems that can adaptively
interact with such behavioral elements.

use the most common and primitive approach,
which involves the generation of signatures of
known malware beforehand and then comparing
newly downloaded executables against these
signatures to predict its nature. This technique
drastically fails in case of any zero-day malware, a
malware which has been newly created and thus a
signature is not available. Other common
techniques are static analysis and dynamic analysis.
Static analysis analyzes the executables without
executing it and predicts the results. It is generally
used because it’s relatively fast but fails if the
malware is packed, encrypted or obfuscated. To
overcome the limitations of static approaches
another approach, i.e., dynamic analysis is used. It
involves collecting behavioural data by executing
the sample in a sandboxed environment and then
using it for detection and classification. The dynamic
analysis also has some limitations such as the
detection of virtual environment and code coverage
issues. As a result, researchers have started using
the combination of both the approaches known as a
hybrid approach.

Game theory, a field which originated in the

The course deals with applications of Markov chains
techniques in certain areas of computer
science and of biology. The unifying aspect in these
applications is the role played by mixing
time analysis, which is the focus of the course.
In a typical combinatorial optimization problem, each
instance x is associated with a state
space Sx, usually of size exponential in the size of
x, where each element of Sx has an
associated cost (or a value). The problem is to nd a
state with minimum cost (or with
maximum value). In the Markov chains approach to
solving such a problem, a Markov
chain is associated with each instance with the
property that the goal state has the highest
probability in the stationary distribution of the chain.
Success of this approach crucially
depends on the mixing time of the associated chain,
that is, how quickly does the chain
come close to its stationary distribution.
Markov chains have also been used to model
evolution for the nite population case lending
themseves to stochastic e ects. For a population of
size N of m types, a state of the chain
is the labelling of the N individuals each into one of
Applications Of Markov the m types. The population goes from

into one of
Applications Of Markov the m types. The population goes from
Chains In Combinatorial 3-0-0-0-9 one state to another through reproduction, mutation,
CS698P
Optimization And In and selection. The speci c way in
Evolutionary Dynamics which each of these happens determine the the
transition probability matrix of the chain.
The result of the evolution modelled by the chain is
given by the stationary distribution
of the chain. In most cases however, it is not known
how to determine the stationary
distribution directly, we need to simulate the chain
`suciently long' and then sample from
the resulting distribution to obtain statistical
properties of the distribution. We need to
determine the mixing time of the chain to nd out how
long is `suciently long'. It has
been established recently that the expected motion
of such evolutionary chains turns out
to be a dynamical system, the trajectory of which
determines the mixing time properties
like rapid mixing.

It is often posed for public consumption as a matter

what resources do organisms have available that let

behavior. Theorists then develop computational
models that capture the quantitative relationship
between these parameters and various
experimental conditions. A good empirical fit permits
further questions of biological and epistemic
plausibility to be asked of the model. Models that
pass these quasi-philosophical checks graduate to
the status of theories. These accounts are,
inevitably, challenged as incomplete or erroneous
by further iterations of experiments and models.

The cycle of research in cognitive science,
